text: Your lungs hold hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs. Normally, they are full of air. But in pneumonia, they fill with fluid and pus. So how does an infection flood the lungs, and why can it be so dangerous?
Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs, the alveoli, in one or both lungs. The sacs fill with fluid, so less oxygen can pass into the blood.

It is caused by germs. Most often bacteria, like Streptococcus pneumoniae. It can also be viruses, like flu, R S V, or COVID nineteen, and less often, fungi. These germs spread through tiny droplets from coughs and sneezes.

When germs reach the alveoli, the immune system fights back. White blood cells rush in, and fluid leaks into the sacs. Air is pushed out, and that part of the lung becomes solid and heavy, like a wet sponge.

The main signs are a cough, often with yellow or green phlegm, fever and chills, shortness of breath, chest pain when breathing or coughing, and tiredness. Older adults may only feel confused or weak.
Anyone can get pneumonia, but some people are at higher risk: young children, adults over sixty five, smokers, and people with asthma, diabetes, heart disease, or a weak immune system.
Doctors listen to the chest for crackling sounds, check oxygen with a finger clip, and take a chest x-ray. On the x-ray, the infected part shows up as a white patch.

Bacterial pneumonia is treated with antibiotics. Take the full course, exactly as prescribed. Viral pneumonia needs rest, fluids, and sometimes antiviral medicine. Severe cases need hospital care and extra oxygen.

You can lower the risk. Vaccines protect against pneumococcus, flu, and COVID. Wash your hands, don't smoke, and cover your coughs. Get urgent help for trouble breathing, blue lips, chest pain, or confusion.

So remember. In pneumonia, infected air sacs fill with fluid, so less oxygen gets in. Watch for cough, fever, and breathlessness. Antibiotics treat the bacterial kind, and vaccines help prevent it. Next, we'll look at COPD, the long term lung disease linked to smoking.
